study.title: Psalm 82 God judges rulers and calls justice
study.overview: Psalm 82 presents God as the supreme judge who stands up in the midst of the assembly of the mighty and condemns magistrates and rulers for their injustice. The center of the psalm is ethical and spiritual: whoever receives authority from God must defend the weak, the orphan and the poor, rather than favor the wicked. The psalm ends with a cry that God publicly assumes the government of the earth, for all nations belong to him.

outline.title: God presides the court and denounces injustice
outline.explanation: The psalmist describes God as a gift among the mighty, not distant from them, but judging his decisions. The denunciation lies on unjust judgments and favoritism toward the wicked, showing that authority without justice affronts the divine government itself.

outline.title: The obligation of rulers: to protect the vulnerable
outline.explanation: The text commands justice to the poor and the orphan, to defend the afflicted and the needy, and to redeem them from the hands of the wicked. The function of power is clearly protective and reparative, not exploitative.

outline.title: Moral Ignorance, Collapse and the sentence of so-called 'gods'
outline.explanation: Those responsible for injustice are described as ignorant and walking in darkness, while the foundations of social order are shaken. Although they have been called 'gods' and 'sons of the Most High', their dignity does not deliver them from death and judgment: they will fall like any man or leader.

outline.title: End appeal: God must judge the whole earth
outline.explanation: The psalm ends with a prayer for God to rise up and judge the whole earth. The reason is that he is the owner of all nations, so no human or local authority has final sovereignty.

study.context: The notes indicate that this psalm deals especially with judges and rulers in courts, and that it could have been used to instruct Israeli magistrates. A proposal of historical context mentions a reform of the courts in the time of Jeosaphah, but this appears only as a possibility, not as a certainty of the text.
study.theology: The psalm affirms the universal sovereignty of God over all human authority. Civil power is not autonomous: it exists under the presence, vigilance and judgment of God. Therefore, social justice is not a peripheral theme, but an expression of the divine reign itself. The text also teaches that privileges of function do not nullify moral responsibility; who represents God's authority should reflect God's character in protecting the weak. The language of 'gods' and 'sons of the Most High' is understood by the commentators as a reference to magistrates invested with delegated authority, but this dignity is temporary and does not prevent death or judgment. The climax of the psalm is the hope that God will fully assume the government of the earth, for all nations already belong to him.

scholarViews.insight: The Psalm denounces those who treat the defenseless with injustice and shows God presiding over the assembly to exercise judgment.
The psalm was thought to instruct magistrates and remember that his office depends on God and should serve the public good.
The final verse is a prayer for God to take over the rule of the earth, for righteousness has been perverted and all nations belong to it.

questions: In what ways can human authority be tempted to favor the wicked rather than to protect the vulnerable?
How does the fact that God judges among the powerful corrects our vision of power, leadership, and responsibility?
Where can we, in a practical way, defend the poor, the orphan and the needy without partiality?
study.practice: This psalm invites the reader to examine any position of influence in the light of God's righteousness. In practice, this means rejecting favoritism, listening attentively to the vulnerable, acting with integrity in public or private decisions and remembering that every authority is provisional. It also calls the church to pray that God governs the nations and for human leaders to be corrected when they depart from righteousness.
study.uncertainty: The exact meaning of 'gods' in 6-7 is interpreted in close but not identical ways: the notes favor the idea of magistrates or rulers as representatives of God, not divine beings. The specific historical context of the psalm is not certain; the association with Jeosaphah reforms is presented only as a hypothesis. The application on the universal expansion of faith in 8 appears in a commentary as prophetic reading, but cannot be treated as the only mandatory conclusion of the text.
